title: Sort with comparator
description: `.sort()` MUTATES and defaults to STRING comparison. Always pass a comparator for numbers.

conversation.intro: How an interview about `.sort()` would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before reaching for `.sort()` — pin down the contract.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I have an array and I want it sorted. A couple of quick questions before I write the call:"

• Are these numbers, strings, or objects? It changes the comparator.
• Do I need ascending or descending order?
• Am I allowed to mutate the input, or do I need a fresh array?
• If two items compare equal, does original order matter (i.e. do I need stable sort)?
sections.why: These are not pedantic questions — each one decides a different line of code. 'Numbers vs strings' is the canonical interview gotcha (`[10, 2, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 10, 2]`); 'mutate or not' decides between `arr.sort(...)` and `[...arr].sort(...)`; 'stable' matters when chaining secondary keys. Asking signals you've been bitten by `.sort()` before.

sections.title: 2. Why this template?
sections.prompt: Name the trap the default `.sort()` walks straight into.
sections.say: "The default `.sort()` with no comparator coerces every element to a string and sorts lexicographically. So `[10, 2, 1].sort()` is `[1, 10, 2]` — because `'10' < '2'` as strings. That's almost never what you want for numbers, so the template is: always pass a comparator. `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers ascending, `(a, b) => b - a` for descending, `(a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)` for strings, and `(a, b) => a.key - b.key` to sort objects by a numeric key."
sections.why: The comparator-always-on-numbers rule is muscle memory. Saying it unprompted before writing the call inoculates against the most-cited JS interview trap. Naming both `a - b` and `localeCompare` shows you know strings have their own canonical path — naive `a < b ? -1 : 1` works but loses locale collation.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — comparator contract
sections.prompt: What does the comparator actually return, and why subtraction?
sections.say:
"The comparator is a function `(a, b) => number` with three legal outcomes:"

• Negative → `a` comes before `b`
• Positive → `b` comes before `a`
• Zero → they're equal (relative order preserved on stable sort)

"That's why `a - b` works for ascending numbers: if `a < b`, `a - b` is negative, so `a` lands first. For descending, flip to `b - a`. The crucial bug to avoid: writing `(a, b) => a > b` looks intuitive but returns true/false → 1/0, never a negative number, so the sort is wrong."
sections.why: Naming the three-valued contract is what distinguishes a candidate from someone who copy-pastes the idiom. The `a > b` boolean-returning bug is the exact thing senior interviewers probe for — they want to see you know WHY subtraction works, not just THAT it does.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the call.
sections.intro: Three cases cover the interesting behaviors — the textbook ascending-numbers case, the descending flip, and the objects-by-key case which is the L3 prompt.

examples.note: Numbers ascending — `a - b` puts smaller first.
examples.trace:
comparator picks pairs:
  3 vs 1 → 3-1=2 positive → 1 before 3
  4 vs 1 → 4-1=3 positive → 1 before 4
  5 vs 4 → 5-4=1 positive → 4 before 5
result: [1,1,3,4,5] (stable — the two 1s keep their original order)

comparator picks pairs:
  3 vs 1 → 1-3=-2 negative → 3 before 1
  4 vs 3 → 3-4=-1 negative → 4 before 3
  5 vs 4 → 4-5=-1 negative → 5 before 4
result: [5,4,3,1,1]

examples.note: Objects-by-key — the L3 pattern. Subtract on the key, not the object.
examples.trace:
comparator picks pair:
  {age:30} vs {age:25} → 30-25=5 positive → {age:25} before {age:30}
result: [{age:25},{age:30}]
(input array is MUTATED — same reference, new order)

sections.why: The third example is the load-bearing one to mention out loud — `(a, b) => a.age - b.age` is the same template applied to a projection. The interviewer is checking whether you know the comparator can project into any numeric field. The mutation note on example 3 is also worth flagging: if the caller still holds the original reference, they'll see it re-ordered.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & pitfalls
sections.prompt: What inputs or comparators would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges and pitfalls worth flagging:"

• Forgot the comparator on numbers → string sort: `[10, 2, 1].sort()` = `[1, 10, 2]`.
• Returned a boolean from the comparator: `(a, b) => a > b` is wrong; coerces to 1/0, never negative.
• Mutates in place → if the caller needs the original, copy first: `[...arr].sort(...)` or `arr.slice().sort(...)`.
• Empty or single-element array → no-op, no error.
• `NaN` values → comparator with `NaN` always returns NaN, which the sort treats as 0 (equal); your NaNs can land anywhere. Worth flagging if floats are in play.
• Strings with mixed locale → use `localeCompare` not `<`, otherwise accented chars sort oddly.
sections.why: The `(a, b) => a > b` bug is the one that catches careless candidates — it's the boolean-coerces-to-0/1 trap that looks right but isn't. Calling it out unprompted is a senior-tier tell. The mutation flag is also high-signal — most candidates forget that `arr.sort()` returns the SAME array, not a new one.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n log n) — V8 uses TimSort, an adaptive merge-insertion hybrid that's stable. The comparator runs O(n log n) times, so the comparator should itself be O(1) — `a - b` and `a.key - b.key` qualify; something like `(a, b) => JSON.stringify(a).localeCompare(JSON.stringify(b))` would secretly make each comparison O(k) where k is the serialized length.

Space is O(log n) auxiliary (TimSort's run stack), but you should treat it as O(n) for safety since engines vary.

The template generalizes: any time you need ordered iteration, sort with a comparator FIRST, then iterate. It's the prep step for two-pointer problems on sorted arrays (3Sum, container-with-most-water) — sorting trades one O(n log n) up front for O(n) sweeps after."
sections.why: Naming TimSort and the comparator-cost gotcha is a senior touch — it shows you think about what the comparator costs PER call, not just the overall sort. The 'sort first, then two-pointer' generalization proves transfer: you see sorting as a primitive that unlocks downstream linear algorithms.

walkthrough.intro: Step through `.sort()` with a comparator on a small array. The trace simulates which pairs the comparator visits and how each return value places the elements. Use ◀ Prev / ▶ Next, or pick a different example.
trace: function* trace(input) {
const dir = input.dir;
const arr = input.arr.map(x => (x && typeof x === 'object') ? { ...x } : x);
yield { line: 1, label: `enter — arr=${JSON.stringify(arr)}, dir=${dir}`, state: { arr: JSON.stringify(arr), dir } };
let cmp, lineForCall;
if (dir === 'asc') { cmp = (a, b) => a - b; lineForCall = 2; }
else if (dir === 'desc') { cmp = (a, b) => b - a; lineForCall = 5; }
else { cmp = (a, b) => a.age - b.age; lineForCall = 11; }
yield { line: lineForCall, label: `pick comparator for dir='${dir}'`, state: { arr: JSON.stringify(arr), dir } };
for (let i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) {
const cur = arr[i];
let j = i - 1;
const curShow = (cur && typeof cur === 'object') ? JSON.stringify(cur) : String(cur);
yield { line: lineForCall, label: `outer step i=${i} — pick cur=${curShow} to insert into sorted prefix`, state: { arr: JSON.stringify(arr), i, cur: curShow } };
while (j >= 0 && cmp(arr[j], cur) > 0) {
const cmpVal = cmp(arr[j], cur);
const ajShow = (arr[j] && typeof arr[j] === 'object') ? JSON.stringify(arr[j]) : String(arr[j]);
yield { line: lineForCall, label: `cmp(${ajShow}, ${curShow}) = ${cmpVal} > 0 → ${ajShow} comes AFTER ${curShow}; shift right`, state: { arr: JSON.stringify(arr), i, j, cmpVal } };
arr[j + 1] = arr[j];
arr[j + 1] = cur;
yield { line: lineForCall, label: `place cur at index ${j + 1} — arr=${JSON.stringify(arr)}`, state: { arr: JSON.stringify(arr), i, placedAt: j + 1 } };
yield { line: lineForCall, label: `sort complete — arr=${JSON.stringify(arr)}`, state: { arr: JSON.stringify(arr), returns: JSON.stringify(arr) } };

notes: .sort MUTATES the original array. Use `[...arr].sort()` if you need a copy.
Default sort converts to string, so `[10, 2, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 2]`.
Comparator returns negative → a first, positive → b first, 0 → equal (order preserved on stable sorts).
Time O(n log n) / Space O(log n) auxiliary (TimSort's run stack).

alternates.label: .toSorted() — non-mutating (ES2023)
alternates.when: Reach for this when the caller must not observe a changed array, or when you're in a functional pipeline where mutation is a bug. Same O(n log n) / O(n) cost as `[...arr].sort()` but cleaner to read.
notes: Returns a NEW sorted array; the input is untouched — unlike `.sort()` which mutates in place.
Available in Node 20+ and all modern browsers (ES2023); polyfill with `[...arr].sort(...)` for older targets.
The comparator syntax is identical to `.sort()` — the only change is the method name.

options: No — returns a new sorted array, like `.map`
Only when the comparator returns 0 for some pair (otherwise it sorts a copy)
Mutates only if the array has more than 10 elements (V8 picks insertion-sort-on-copy below that threshold)

questions.q: A comparator returning a negative number means:
options: Skip this pair — the sort tries again with a different pivot
Sorts in descending order, regardless of which arg is bigger

questions.q: You need the sorted result but must NOT change the original array. Which is correct?
questions.explain: `.sort()` mutates in place, so copy first with `[...arr]` (or `arr.slice()`); there is no non-mutating `.sorted()` on arrays.

questions.q: You write `(a, b) => a > b` as a numeric comparator. What's the bug?
options: It returns a boolean (true/false), which coerces to 1/0 — it never returns a negative, so the sort order is unreliable
questions.explain: A comparator must return negative/zero/positive; `a > b` yields true/false → 1/0, never negative, so equal-or-less cases are indistinguishable and ordering is broken.

questions.q: Two objects compare equal under your comparator. A 'stable' sort guarantees what about them?
options: They are coalesced — only the first instance is kept, the rest are dropped
Their relative order from the input is preserved
They are grouped together but their internal order depends on the sort algorithm chosen at runtime
Stability only applies when sorting primitives; objects always sort in unspecified order
questions.explain: Stability means equal elements keep their original relative order — modern V8 `.sort()` is stable, which matters when sorting by a secondary key after a primary one.

L3.prompt: Write `sortByAge(arr)` returning the array sorted by `.age` ascending. Log `JSON.stringify(sortByAge([{name:"A",age:30},{name:"B",age:25}]))`.
